In a haloarene the lone pair on the halogen is delocalised into the ring, so the C-X bond acquires partial double bond character: it is shorter, stronger and far less willing to break heterolytically than the ordinary polar single bond of an alkyl halide. Both aryl compounds (I) and (II) must therefore be **less** reactive towards a nucleophile than both alkyl compounds (III) and (IV). That rules out the two orders that place the alkyl halides at the bottom, namely III < IV < II < I and IV < III < I < II.

Between the two haloarenes, section 10.6.1 states that an electron withdrawing group at the ortho and/or para position greatly increases the reactivity of a haloarene. Compound (II) carries an \(\mathrm{NO_2}\) group para to the halogen, which withdraws electron density and stabilises the intermediate formed on nucleophilic attack, so (II) is more reactive than the plain halobenzene (I). That rules out the order II < I < III < IV.

The only remaining order is **I < II < III < IV**. Within the alkyl pair it places the secondary halide \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH-X}\) above the tertiary \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-X}\), which is the order expected for direct attack of a nucleophile on the carbon: the three methyl groups of the tertiary halide crowd the pentacoordinate transition state.

The peroxide (Kharasch) effect — anti-Markownikov addition through a free radical chain — is observed **only with \(\mathrm{HBr}\)**. With \(\mathrm{HI}\) the chain cannot be sustained, so the presence of peroxide changes nothing and the addition follows Markownikov's rule: hydrogen adds to the doubly bonded carbon that already carries more hydrogens (the terminal \(\mathrm{CH_2}\)) and iodine adds to the middle carbon.

The major product is therefore \(\mathrm{CH_3-CHI-CH_3}\), 2-iodopropane.

The other choices fail on inspection: \(\mathrm{I-CH_2-CH=CH_2}\) still contains the double bond, so it is a substitution product and not an addition product at all; \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2I}\) is the anti-Markownikov product, which would require the peroxide effect to operate for \(\mathrm{HI}\); and \(\mathrm{CH_3-CHI-CH_2OH}\) contains oxygen, for which the reaction mixture provides no source.

Racemization is observed only when **both** conditions hold: the carbon carrying the halogen is a chiral carbon, and the substitution goes through the \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) route, whose planar carbocation intermediate can be attacked by the nucleophile from either face (section 10.6.3).

In \(\mathrm{CH_3-CHCl-C_2H_5}\) (compound I) the carbon bearing chlorine is bonded to \(\mathrm{CH_3}\), \(\mathrm{C_2H_5}\), \(\mathrm{H}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl}\) — four different groups — so it is a chiral carbon, and being a secondary halide it can ionise to a carbocation. Alkaline hydrolysis therefore gives both enantiomers of the alcohol in nearly equal amount, that is, a racemic product. So only compound I is likely to racemize.

Benzyl chloride \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-CH_2Cl}\) (II) does form a resonance stabilised carbocation easily, but its \(\mathrm{CH_2}\) carbon carries two hydrogens and is not chiral, so there is no configuration to invert and nothing to observe. The same objection applies to \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(CH_3)-CH_2Cl}\) (IV). Chlorobenzene (III) is a haloarene and does not undergo alkaline hydrolysis under these conditions at all.

Alkyl fluorides are best prepared by the **Swartz reaction**: an alkyl chloride or bromide is heated with a metallic fluoride such as \(\mathrm{AgF}\), \(\mathrm{Hg_2F_2}\), \(\mathrm{CoF_2}\) or \(\mathrm{SbF_3}\), and the halogen is exchanged for fluorine.

The Finkelstein reaction is the corresponding exchange with \(\mathrm{NaI}\) in dry acetone and yields alkyl **iodides**, not fluorides. Direct free radical fluorination of an alkane is violently exothermic and almost impossible to control, so it gives a mixture of products rather than a clean alkyl fluoride. Sandmeyer's reaction converts a diazonium salt into an **aryl** chloride or bromide using \(\mathrm{CuCl}\)/\(\mathrm{CuBr}\), so it makes neither an alkyl halide nor a fluoride.

A molecule is chiral when it contains a carbon bonded to four **different** groups (section 10.5.1).

In **2-bromobutane**, \(\mathrm{CH_3-CHBr-CH_2-CH_3}\), carbon 2 carries \(\mathrm{CH_3}\), \(\mathrm{C_2H_5}\), \(\mathrm{H}\) and \(\mathrm{Br}\) — all four different — so it is a chiral carbon and the molecule is chiral. It is the exact bromine analogue of 2-chlorobutane, the chapter's own worked example of a pair of enantiomers.

In 1-bromobutane, \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2Br}\), the carbon bearing bromine also carries two hydrogens, so it is not a chiral carbon. In 1,1-dibromobutane the same carbon carries two identical bromine atoms, again ruling out chirality. 2,3-Dibromobutane does contain two such carbons, but that name also covers the meso form, which has an internal mirror plane and is optically inactive, so it is not an unambiguously chiral molecule.

[Textbook misprint: the fourth alternative is printed as \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(CH_3)-CH(CH_3)-CHCl}\), whose last carbon is written \(\mathrm{CHCl}\) and so has only three bonds. It is transcribed exactly as printed. Read as the intended \(\mathrm{CH_2Cl}\) it would be 1-chloro-2,3-dimethylbutane, which is a six-carbon halide and still fails the question's own test, since reduction would give 2,3-dimethylbutane \(\mathrm{C_6H_{14}}\) and not \(\mathrm{C_5H_{12}}\). The answer is unaffected either way.]

Wurtz reaction couples two molecules of the alkyl halide through sodium, giving the symmetrical alkane \(\mathrm{R-R}\). The product 2,2,5,5-tetramethylhexane is \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-CH_2-CH_2-C(CH_3)_3}\); cutting it in half at the central bond gives \(\mathrm{R} = \mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-CH_2-}\), the neopentyl group. The alkyl chloride is therefore \(\mathrm{CH_3-C(CH_3)_2-CH_2Cl}\), neopentyl chloride.

This is confirmed by the second clue: reduction with zinc-copper couple replaces the halogen by hydrogen, giving \(\mathrm{R-H} = \mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-CH_3}\), neopentane, whose molecular formula is \(\mathrm{C_5H_{12}}\) as stated.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CCl(CH_3)-CH_2CH_3}\) satisfies the second clue (its reduction gives 2-methylbutane, also \(\mathrm{C_5H_{12}}\)) but fails the first, because coupling it gives 3,3,4,4-tetramethylhexane, not the compound named. \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CHCl-CH_3}\) has only four carbons, so its reduction gives butane and not \(\mathrm{C_5H_{12}}\). The remaining choice has six carbons, so its reduction gives 2,3-dimethylbutane, \(\mathrm{C_6H_{14}}\), which again contradicts the stated formula.

In a nitrile the carbon of the \(\mathrm{-C \equiv N}\) group is counted as carbon 1 of the chain, so butanenitrile is \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-C \equiv N}\) and the alkyl group attached to cyanide has only **three** carbons. It is made by heating **n-propyl chloride with KCN**, where the cyanide ion attacks the carbon bearing chlorine in a nucleophilic substitution and displaces chloride.

Heating n-butyl chloride with KCN would attach cyanide to a four-carbon group and give \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2C \equiv N}\), which is pentanenitrile. Propanol and butanol cannot be used at all: the \(\mathrm{-OH}\) group is not a leaving group, so alcohols do not undergo nucleophilic substitution with KCN.

An \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) reaction has the heterolysis of the C-X bond as its slow step, so its rate is decided by the stability of the carbocation formed. Stability, and hence \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) rate, runs tertiary > secondary > primary (section 10.6.4).

In **2-iodo-2-methylbutane** the iodine sits on a carbon joined to three other carbons, so ionisation gives a tertiary carbocation — the most stable of the four, and the fastest to form.

2-Iodo-3-methylbutane gives only a secondary carbocation. 1-Iodobutane and 1-iodopropane both carry the iodine on a terminal \(\mathrm{CH_2}\) group and would have to form a primary carbocation, which is the least stable, so these two react slowest by this route.

Cyclohexyl chloride reacts with magnesium in dry ether to give the Grignard reagent cyclohexylmagnesium chloride, \(\mathrm{C_6H_{11}-MgCl}\); this is the intermediate 'A'.

The carbon joined to magnesium in a Grignard reagent is strongly nucleophilic and behaves like a carbanion, so water protonates it at once — this is why Grignard reactions must be run under anhydrous conditions. Hydrolysis therefore replaces the \(\mathrm{-MgCl}\) by \(\mathrm{-H}\), and the product 'B' is **cyclohexane**, \(\mathrm{C_6H_{12}}\), the plain saturated ring with no substituent.

The two choices that still contain magnesium describe the Grignard reagent itself, so they are 'A' rather than 'B'. The choice carrying both chlorine and magnesium on the ring is formed at no stage of this sequence, since only one chlorine was present to begin with and it is consumed in making the Grignard reagent.

**Chloroform** is the source of dichlorocarbene. On warming with aqueous or alcoholic potassium hydroxide it loses the elements of \(\mathrm{HCl}\), \(\mathrm{CHCl_3} + \mathrm{KOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{:CCl_2} + \mathrm{KCl} + \mathrm{H_2O}\), giving the electron deficient reactive intermediate dichlorocarbene, \(\mathrm{:CCl_2}\).

Tetrachloromethane cannot do this because it has no hydrogen at all, so there is no \(\mathrm{HCl}\) to eliminate. Iodoform, \(\mathrm{CHI_3}\), has the right shape but would release diiodocarbene, \(\mathrm{:CI_2}\), not dichlorocarbene. DDT is a finished polyhalogen insecticide with no such acidic hydrogen and is not used as a carbene source.
